articles.title: Struggling with depression? Psychiatrist says 6 habits may be making it worse
articles.summary: Dr. Daniel Amen reveals the everyday habits that worsen depression, from alcohol use and isolation to processed foods and unchecked negative thoughts.
articles.body: Depression rates among Americans ages 12 and older rose nearly 60% over a decade, increasing from 8.2% in 2013–2014 to 13.1% in 2021–2023, according to a recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Finding the right treatment for depression can take time, and antidepressants usually take four to eight weeks to work, per the National Institute of Mental Health. For those struggling with the condition, clinical psychiatrist Dr. Daniel Amen – founder of Amen Clinics in California – says avoiding the following habits may help to manage symptoms and support mental health. IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE No. 1: Drinking alcohol Alcohol may offer temporary relief from depression symptoms, but as its effects wear off, mood can worsen. As the brain adjusts to alcohol’s relaxing effects, it can leave people feeling more anxious and restless after the buzz fades, making them feel "worse than before," Amen warned. Drinking can also disrupt sleep, adding to next-day fatigue, according to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism. No. 2: Staying in bed It might be tempting to linger in bed when you wake up, but Amen encouraged people with depression to get up and start their day. "When people are depressed, they tend to have pretty low activity, especially in the front part of their brain, but burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse," he said. "Get up, get out." SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES Amen's advice aligns with a broader approach called behavioral activation, a type of therapy that helps people gradually return to meaningful activities rather than withdraw from them. Behavioral activation has been shown to be beneficial for treating depression, according to a 2020 Cochrane review of 53 studies involving 5,495 adults. No. 3: Believing your negative thoughts A negative mindset can make it easier to believe things that aren’t true — or, as Amen puts it, every "stupid" thought. He refers to these as "ANTs," or automatic negative thoughts. "The thoughts that come into your mind automatically and ruin your day – they drive depression," he said. "Burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse … get up, get out." When feeling strong emotions – such as sadness, anger, anxiety or just lack of control – Amen recommends writing down what you’re thinking and then asking yourself if it’s true. "My favorite part – and there's a whole method to this – is flipping the thought and actually meditating on the opposite of the thought you have," he said. "So, taking each thought captive." No. 4: Isolating yourself Depression can lead people to withdraw from others, but social isolation may worsen symptoms, Amen said. "The more isolated you get, the louder the ANT chorus gets, and it makes [depression] worse," he cautioned. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER A 2025 study published in General Hospital Psychiatry tracked more than 339,000 U.K. adults for roughly 12 years. Loneliness was associated with a 77% higher risk of developing depression, while social isolation was linked to a 14% higher risk. No. 5: Eating highly processed foods Eating more ultraprocessed foods, including many fast-food items, has been linked to a higher risk of depression, Amen said, although research has not established cause and effect. "There's actually a lot of consensus now among psychiatrists that inflammation drives certain types of depression," the doctor told Fox News Digital. A 2025 review in the American Journal of Psychiatry supports inflammation’s role in some cases, but notes that elevated inflammatory markers occurred in only a subset of people with depression. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Amen recommends adhering to an anti-inflammatory diet emphasizing "vegetables, healthy protein and healthy fats." A 2024 review of five randomized trials involving 1,507 adults found that Mediterranean-style diets reduced depressive symptoms compared with control groups, although results varied considerably among studies. No. 6: Taking medication without a proper assessment Depression treatment is individualized, so not every medication is right for everyone — and not every patient requires medication. Amen emphasized the importance of receiving a thorough assessment prior to receiving antidepressants, which he said can be "lifesaving." For milder depression, psychotherapy is often the first approach. People with moderate or severe depression are usually prescribed medication as part of their initial treatment plan, according to the National Institute of Mental Health. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For those who have done "all the right things" but still struggle, Amen encouraged seeking further medical evaluation. Depending on symptoms and medical history, a clinician may order blood tests to check for conditions such as anemia or thyroid disease that could contribute to symptoms. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The doctor also recommended considering approaches beyond medication, such as exercise — or, as Amen suggested, "walking like you're late" — which has been proven in studies to perform better than some depression medications. Some supplements, like omega-3 and saffron, have been found to be more effective than antidepressants in recent research.

articles.title: 9 Healthy Pasta Toppings to Keep You Full and Stabilize Blood Sugar, From Dietitians
articles.summary: What you top pasta with can make a big nutritional difference.. Dietitians share their favorite high-protein, high-fiber pasta toppings to balance blood sugar and keep you full.
articles.body: Pasta is one of life’s simple pleasures. It’s versatile, delicious and often fit for the pickiest of eaters. However, this pantry staple can get a bad rap for being high in carbohydrates and less nutrient-dense than other whole grains. In recent years, the better-for-you pasta market has exploded. At the grocery store, you’ll find countless high-protein, nutrient-fortified alternatives made with whole grains or legumes. There’s chickpea pasta, black bean pasta and brown rice pasta. These are often marketed as being healthier than traditional pasta, which is made with durum semolina wheat. However, many dietitians argue that there’s nothing inherently bad or unhealthy about regular pasta. And what you add to a bowl of pasta likely makes a bigger nutritional difference than the ingredients of the noodles, experts say. Is Regular Pasta Good for You? “Do not be afraid of pasta. Yes, it’s a carbohydrate, but it can still be a good addition to your diet and should not be avoided,” Sibylle Kranz, Ph.D., registered dietitian nutritionist and spokesperson for the Obesity Society, tells TODAY.com. You can still enjoy regular pasta as part of a healthy diet — and many people do around the world. “Pasta is an excellent ingredient and base for balanced, nutrient-rich meals,” Frances Largeman-Roth, registered dietitian and author, tells TODAY.com. It’s a good source of carbohydrates, which are the body’s main source of energy, along with other beneficial vitamins and minerals. “Regular enriched pasta is fortified with folate, iron, thiamin and riboflavin, which can help you meet your requirements for these micronutrients,” says Largeman-Roth. Cooked wheat pasta also contains some resistant starch, a type of carbohydrate that gets fermented in the colon. “It acts like fiber in the gut, helping us to feel full,” Largeman-Roth adds. Cooling pasta after cooking can significantly increase the resistant starch content, so your leftovers may be even healthier. When it comes to pasta, moderation is key, Kranz says. It’s important to stick to the recommended serving size, which varies depending on the pasta shape. The Healthiest Pasta Toppings What you put on top of pasta is just as important as, if not more important than, the type of pasta you use, the experts note. Any pasta can be made healthier by adding whole foods like lean meats, vegetables, legumes and nuts. “Pasta is more filling with the addition of protein, fiber and healthy fats,” Largeman-Roth explains. On its own, regular pasta does not contain all nine essential amino acids. “It’s good to add a topping or a sauce that also has amino acids to make (the pasta) a complete protein,” Kranz adds. What you top pasta with can also impact how the body digests the carbohydrates. “Research shows that after consumption of refined grain pasta, blood glucose increases and there’s an insulin spike. After, the glucose is removed from the bloodstream relatively fast, so there’s this steep drop,” Kranz explains. Foods rich in protein and fiber will help slow down digestion and stabilize blood sugar, which curbs hunger later on. Here are 9 of the healthiest pasta toppings, according to dietitians: Shrimp If you’re looking for a higher-protein pasta, adding shrimp is a no-brainer. They’re one of the healthiest types of seafood and easy to cook, which makes them a popular choice among dietitians. One serving of cooked shrimp provides about 25 grams of complete protein for only 100 calories. Shrimp are also a good source of B vitamins, iodine and selenium, a mineral that supports thyroid health and immune function. The shells get their pink color from astaxanthin, a potent antioxidant. “I like penne with sautéed shrimp, peas and Manchego cheese,” Largeman-Roth says. Lentils Lentils are a versatile and often overlooked topping for pasta, according to registered dietitian and TODAY.com nutrition editor Natalie Rizzo. These tiny legumes are loaded with nutrients. They stand out for their impressive protein and fiber content, which is why lentils are Rizzo’s favorite plant protein to help balance blood sugar. One cup of cooked lentils provides about 18 grams of protein and a whopping 16 grams of fiber (nearly half the daily value). Rizzo recommends using lentils in bolognese instead of ground meat. Cruciferous Vegetables “Adding any vegetables is always a good start,” says Kranz. Cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts are a dietitian favoritie because they’re loaded with gut-healthy fiber, vitamins and antioxidants. These make pasta more filling, stabilize blood sugar and provide beneficial micronutrients. Broccoli, for example, is high in glucosinolates, plant compounds which may have anti-cancer properties, says Rizzo. “Small pasta shapes, like orrechiette, are a wonderful base for cooked broccoli and Brussels sprouts,” says Largeman-Roth. Nuts Nuts are an important source of healthy unsaturated fats, plant protein and fiber. Whole nuts can add texture and flavor to pasta, but nut-based sauces offer more nutritional bang for your buck, the experts note. Pesto is a classic sauce that’s loaded with heart-healthy nuts, fresh basil and extra virgin olive oil, making it an “ideal” healthy pasta topping, says Kranz. Pesto can be made with pine nuts, walnuts or pistachios, which all provide protein and heart-healthy fatty acids. Greek Yogurt Yes, Greek yogurt belongs on pasta. The tangy dairy staple is a nutritious alternative to cream sauces. Greek yogurt is packed with filling protein, offering about 15 grams per serving, and naturally low in calories. It’s also loaded with calcium, which helps build and maintain strong bones, plus probiotics to support digestive health, says Rizzo. Mix Greek yogurt with fresh herbs, spices and aromatics or add it to any sauce for a creamy, high-protein twist. Tinned Fish Canned tuna, salmon and sardines are high-protein, budget-friendly pasta toppings dietitians love. Salmon and sardines are particularly rich in essential omega-3 fatty acids, which support brain function and heart health, says Largeman-Roth. Tuna stands out for its lean protein content. You can add tinned fish to tomato-based sauces or mix it directly with pasta. “I like tossing pasta with salmon and asparagus, plus lemon zest and EVOO,” says Largeman-Roth. White Beans If you follow a plant-based diet, blended white beans are an excellent creamy dairy substitute. Cannellini and navy varieties are some of the highest-fiber beans you can eat, offering nearly 10 grams per serving, TODAY.com reported previously. The combination of fiber and plant protein helps slow digestion and balance blood sugar. Plus, white beans are rich in potassium, a mineral that supports healthy blood pressure and muscles. Rizzo combines pureed white beans with canned pumpkin for a hearty, fall-inspired pasta sauce. Dark Leafy Greens Dark leafy greens are a quick, easy way to add dietary fiber and micronutrients to pasta. Dietitian favorites include baby spinach, Swiss chard and kale. These nutrient-dense greens are loaded with insoluble fiber, which adds bulk to stool and aids digestion. Most leafy greens are rich in vitamins A, C and K, along with essential minerals like iron and magnesium. These wilt when heated, so you can add a high volume of fresh leafy greens directly to any pasta dish. Squash Squash is another delicious pasta topping that will add a boost of nutrients, the experts say. Butternut, delicata and summer squash are all excellent sources of fiber to support digestive health and easy to blend into sauces. Most squash varieties are rich in beta-carotene, a precursor to vitamin A which supports eye and skin health. “My favorite combo is delicata squash and mushrooms with grated ricotta salata and toasted walnuts,” says Largeman-Roth. Least Healthy Pasta Toppings There’s no pasta topping you need to avoid entirely, unless you’re allergic to an ingredient, says Kranz. However, some popular choices should be limited to an occasional treat. These include sauces made with heavy cream or butter. “Alfredo and Bechamel-based sauces tend to be very rich and very high in saturated fat,” says Kranz. Processed red meats like bacon and sausage are also high in unhealthy fats and cholesterol. “Use sound judgment with these,” says Kranz. Is It Healthy to Eat Pasta Every Day? It can be healthy to eat pasta daily, especially if you pair it with nutritious toppings, the experts note. “While you can certainly eat pasta as part of a meal each day, I like to see more variety in someone’s diet,” says Largeman-Roth. Try switching up your carbohydrate sources by rotating pasta with brown rice, quinoa or potatoes.

articles.title: Poland shooting: Surgeon who assisted wounded police officer 'undoubtedly saved his life'
articles.summary: One of the men, Professor Michal Pędziwiatr, when they got to the scene, they treated both the alleged gunman and the police officers.
articles.body:
One of the two surgeons who rushed to save lives in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Poland says his colleague stopped the bleeding of the police officer, "undoubtedly" saving his life.

Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reports.

"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," Pędziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.

Pędziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.

"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who."

Police are continuing to investigate Saturday's incident after six people were killed in the Krakow's market square. Sixteen more were injured, including Senior Police Constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański.

Three other bodies were found in the alleged gunman's apartment who were identified by police as the suspect's parents and sister.

Wounded police officers 'saved many lives'

Once the shooting stopped, Pędziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the apparent perpetrator who needed help, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.

"He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt.

"If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance".

Meanwhile, Pędziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located.

"I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt.

According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.

Four women and two men were among those killed, including four polish nationals, a British man and a non-Polish citizen whose nationality has not yet been disclosed.

The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland is launching an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.

Separately, six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers reportedly also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.

James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square when the shooting happened.

The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".

articles.title: Shivabagh residents flag damaged road, demand repairs
articles.summary: Shivabagh residents demand urgent road repairs in Mangaluru as potholes, dug-up stretches and sewage overflow persist amid delayed UGD and footpath work.
articles.body: Mangaluru: Residents of Shivabagh are demanding urgent repairs to the badly damaged road, which has become a major inconvenience for motorists and pedestrians due to massive potholes, dug-up stretches and overflowing sewage. The road, an important link connecting Pumpwell, Bendoor and Kadri, also provides access to the local ESI hospital.Residents alleged that despite repeated complaints and inspections by elected representatives and Mangaluru City Corporation (MCC) officials, no concrete action has been taken for the past four to five months."The situation here has been like this for so many months now. The MLA, former corporator and MCC officials havejust come for inspection and gone without any proper resolution to the problem," a local shopkeeper said.Echoing the concerns, a resident said, "We have raised complaints many times to authorities and written letters, yet it's been more than 4-5 months now and no action has been taken."The situation has been further aggravated by incomplete footpath construction, with certain stretches standing nearly a foot higher than the road, posing a risk to pedestrians. Incomplete underground drainage (UGD) work has also resulted in sewage flowing onto the road, raising concerns over public health and hygiene.During his visit to the area on Thursday, MLC Ivan D'Souza highlighted the importance of Shivabagh main road, stating that it connects Canara Club to the national highway and serves as a key stretch up to Karnataka Bank. He said major UGD and footpath drain works had been undertaken in the area. articles.title: Kasaragod teen sustains injury as revolver goes off accidentally
articles.summary: Kasaragod: 17-year-old injured as revolver kept under pillow accidentally discharges; Bekal police book father for negligent storage under BNS and Arms Act.
articles.body: Kozhikode: A 17-year-old boy sustained serious injuries after a revolver kept under a pillow at his house accidentally went off while he was examining the firearm at Poochakkad in Kasaragod. The injured has been identified as Afas Ahammed, a resident of Solar Mahal at Poochakkad in Pallikkara, under the limits of Bekal police station.The incident occurred around 9.30pm on Saturday when the boy reportedly took the revolver, which had been kept under a pillow in the bedroom, and was examining it. The firearm accidentally discharged, with the bullet piercing his stomach and leaving him seriously injured. Afas is undergoing treatment at a private hospital in Kasaragod.Bekal police have registered a case against his father, Kunjahammed, who holds the firearm licence, for allegedly storing the weapon negligently.The case has been registered under Section 125(b) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with acts of rashness or negligence endangering human life, and Section 30 of the Arms Act, pertaining to violations of licence conditions. articles.title: Pro-life pregnancy center expands mission to help patients embrace their God-given gender
articles.summary: By listening to the Holy Spirit, Heidi Matzke, executive director of the Alternatives Pregnancy Center, said her clinic helps women embrace the gender they were given by God.
articles.body: Helping a transgender man detransition to being a woman again is not something the pro-life, gospel-led Alternatives Pregnancy Center even notes on its website. But because it is a full-service women's health clinic with doctors who specialize in hormone therapy, it's simply something they do in order to give women the care they need to fully embrace their God-given gender. It is all based on listening to the Holy Spirit, said executive director Heidi Matzke. STUDY REVEALS UNEXPECTED HEALTH BENEFITS AFTER 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER Based in Sacramento, California, Alternatives is one of hundreds of like-minded pregnancy help centers across the country. These venues may have different names, but they all work to help women with unplanned pregnancies. Still, years ago when Matzke took over, she knew she needed help — heavenly help. Matzke told Fox News, "When God called me into this ministry ... I felt the Holy Spirit impress upon my heart back then, 'Heidi, you're right. You have no idea what you're doing, and that's why you'd better be face-down before me every single day. You better be fasting and praying.'" She did fast. And she prayed and listened, she said. The result today is a pregnancy help center that is also a full-service health clinic for women. New challenges It wasn't long before another challenge came Matzke's way, involving listening to God. She asked the Holy Spirit to direct her very short talk at a church soon after launching the full-service clinic. The pastor gave her just two minutes. By listening to the Holy Spirit, Heidi Matzke became the angel in Jessica Rose's life. Matzke heard the Holy Spirit say to talk only about the women's health services the center offered and nothing else — not even the unplanned pregnancy help. Then, between services, a man dressed as a woman came to her in the pews. It was just the two of them. He said the words that changed both their lives. He said to her, "What you don't know about me is that I'm biologically female, and I encountered Christ. The Holy Spirit has done work in my heart, and I am now trying to detransition. But my current doctors have basically abandoned me and I have nowhere to go." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH NEWS That "man dressed as a woman" was Jessica Rose. Her story is all over the internet. On that faith-filled day, Rose told Matzke she had been sobbing uncontrollably during Matzke's short presentation, as she had been praying that morning that God would provide her with free women's medical care. By listening to the Holy Spirit, Matzke became the angel in Jessica Rose's life. Her doctors had been eager to start her on hormones and surgery to remove her breasts after just a 30-minute consultation. The women's heath clinic at that moment became more full-service than Heidi Matzke could ever imagine. It became a place where all women, meaning adult females, can be strengthened and shown to love themselves as they are in the light of the Gospel of Christ. On an episode of the "Lighthouse Faith" podcast, Matzke talks about her encounter with Jessica Rose. articles.title: Altnagelvin Hospital: Female paramedic sustains multiple injuries in assault
articles.summary: The NI Ambulance Service said the paramedic sustained injuries to the back of her head, neck, face, and hands during the incident.
articles.body:
A female paramedic has been seriously assaulted at Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry while responding to someone in need of medical assistance.

Police said the attack happened at about 17:45 GMT on Saturday and a suspect has been identified.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said the paramedic sustained injuries to the back of her head, neck, face and hands during the attack. They said she is also believed "to have suffered concussion".

They added that the incident happened after the NIAS received a call to provide medical assistance to a male patient who was being transported by ambulance to the hospital, following initial treatment.

The NIAS said the "attack lasted a number of minutes".

"On arrival at the hospital, and while being transferred from the stretcher to the chair, the patient delivered a punch to the face of one of the paramedics who was helping him".

"The force of the blow knocked her down and knocked her glasses off her face," they said.

"The other paramedic tried as best she could to intervene but couldn't get into a proper position to help, after the assailant also attempted to punch her.

"He then turned his attention back to the first paramedic and started a sustained attack on her as she lay helpless."

Jenny Keane, chief executive of the NIAS, said she was "horrified and outraged" to hear of the assault.

"This incident is particularly disturbing given that it was perpetrated by an adult male on a female paramedic, while her other female colleagues did what they could to help.

"This was a sustained assault on a paramedic who has a career of over 37 years, caring for her local community.

"Although her physical injuries, of which there are many, may heal over the coming days and weeks, I would be concerned at the psychological and emotional impact this may have on her and others involved."

Keane said NIAS staff "must be free to go anywhere without the fear of being assaulted, quite simply for delivering care and compassion to someone they have been called to assist".

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) Foyle assembly member Sinéad McLaughlin, who knows the paramedic personally, said she was "absolutely appalled by this vicious attack on a woman".

She said she found the incident and the extent of the paramedic's injuries "deeply upsetting".

"We cannot allow attacks on healthcare workers to become something that is simply accepted as part of the job.

"We need to send a clear message that this will not be tolerated, and the safety of our frontline workers must be a priority."

Sinn Féin assembly member Philip McGuigan said there must be "zero tolerance" of attacks or abuse against health and social care workers.

"Reports of this attack are deeply disturbing.

"Health service workers go above and beyond to save lives and keep people safe, often working in very challenging circumstances," he added.

"They, and all workers, should never have to face abuse, attack, intimidation or threats in the workplace."

articles.title: Forget prunes: Popular green fruit shows promise for constipation relief
articles.summary: A review of 33 studies links eating two green kiwis daily for four weeks to more regular bowel movements in people with constipation or IBS-C.
articles.body: Eating two green kiwis a day could help people struggling with constipation, a new review suggests. The research, published in the journal Food, Nutrition and Health, looked at 33 previous studies and reports on kiwifruit and digestive health. Eating two fresh green kiwis a day for about four weeks was linked to more regular bowel movements, less straining and better digestive comfort in people with constipation or irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C). COMMON KITCHEN STAPLE MAY HELP RELIEVE MILD CONSTIPATION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS In one international trial included in the review, people with constipation had about 1.5 more complete bowel movements per week, while those with IBS-C had about 1.7 more per week. Both groups also reported improved digestive comfort. The new review suggests there may be several reasons kiwi helps with constipation. Its fiber can add bulk and hold water in stool, while the fruit's natural water and sorbitol may help make stool easier to pass. Researchers said the benefit likely comes from several parts of the whole fruit working together rather than one component alone. Kiwi was not necessarily more effective than other constipation treatments. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ One U.S. trial included in the review found that green kiwi, psyllium fiber and prunes all helped improve chronic constipation. Kiwi was associated with fewer side effects and was well-tolerated by many participants. The evidence is strongest for fresh green kiwi, the researchers noted. There is less research on gold kiwi, powders and extracts, so those forms should not be assumed to have the same effect. Jason Heiselman, a New York-based certified nutritionist and professional chef at Hungryroot in New York City, previously told Fox News Digital that kiwi is an easy fruit to work into a person's diet. "It feels like a no-brainer to include a few slices with any meal," said Heiselman, who was not involved in the new review. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Kiwi contains fiber along with a natural enzyme called actinidin, which can help with digestion, the nutritionist noted. "Pairing kiwi with some good fat sources, like seeds, nuts or full-fat dairy, allows your body to absorb more nutrients," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER For people who do not want to eat kiwi on its own, the fruit can also work in savory meals, according to Heiselman. "Raw kiwi slices often make their way to my dinner table," he said. Heiselman said he pairs the fruit with salty cheeses, toasted pistachios and shaved red onion, and has also used kiwi as the base for chutneys and relishes. There were some limitations to the findings. The paper reviewed previous research rather than conducting a new clinical trial, and the studies differed in the people involved, the types and amounts of kiwi consumed, and the results researchers measured. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Most of the research also looked at relatively short periods of time, so more studies are needed to determine whether the benefits continue long-term. Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment. Andrea Margolis of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.
